items.prompt: What should you do when you speak to a group?

options.text: Look at the floor the whole time.
options.why: Your listeners like to see your face.

options.text: Look at your listeners and speak clearly.
Speak as fast as you can.
options.why: Very fast talking is hard to follow.

options.text: Cover your mouth with your hand.
options.why: This makes your voice hard to hear.

hints: Think about a good speaker you have watched.
How can you help people hear and follow you?
Imagine you are in the audience. What would help you?
items.explanation: Looking at your listeners and speaking clearly helps them hear you and feel that you are talking to them.

items.prompt: Your friend is giving a talk. What does a good listener do?

options.text: talks to the person next to them
options.why: This makes it hard for others to hear.

options.text: looks out of the window
options.why: You might miss what your friend says.

options.text: watches the speaker and stays quiet
plays with a pencil
options.why: Fiddling shows you are not listening.

hints: Think about how you want people to act when you speak.
Good listening uses your eyes and your ears.
Which answer shows the speaker you care about their talk?
items.explanation: Good listeners look at the speaker and stay quiet, so they can hear and think of questions.

items.prompt: Which is a good question to ask after a talk about turtles?

options.text: How many eggs does a turtle lay?
What did you have for breakfast?
options.why: This question is not about the talk.

options.text: Can I go now?
options.why: This does not show interest in the talk.

options.text: Why is your bag blue?
options.why: This question is not about turtles.

hints: A good question is about the topic of the talk.
Which question would help you learn more about turtles?
Cross out the questions that are not about turtles.
items.explanation: A good question is about the talk and helps you learn more, like asking how many eggs a turtle lays.

items.prompt: You are telling the class how to make a paper boat. Which words help your listeners follow the steps?

options.text: big, small, red, blue
options.why: These describe things. They do not show the order.

options.text: happy, sad, cross, tired
options.why: These are feelings, not order words.

options.text: and, and, and, and
options.why: Saying and again and again is hard to follow.

options.text: first, next, then, finally

hints: Instructions must be done in order.
Which words show what comes first and what comes after?
Think of the words a recipe uses.
items.explanation: First, next, then and finally are order words. They help listeners follow each step.

items.prompt: When you read a poem aloud, how can you make it more interesting to listen to?

options.text: Read every word in the same flat voice.
options.why: A flat voice can make a poem sound dull.

options.text: Change your voice to match the feelings in the poem.
Read as fast as you can.
options.why: Listeners need time to enjoy the words.

options.text: Whisper so that nobody can hear.
options.why: Your listeners need to hear the poem.

hints: Think about how a storyteller makes a story exciting.
Can your voice be loud, soft, fast or slow?
How would you read a happy line? How would you read a sad one?
items.explanation: Changing your voice to match the feelings, and pausing at the right moments, makes a poem come alive for listeners.

items.prompt: Tell us about your favourite food. Say what it is, what it tastes like and when you eat it.

criteria.label: I spoke clearly and loudly enough
I said what the food is, how it tastes and when I eat it
I used describing words, like crunchy or sweet

hints: Think of your food before you start.
Use describing words like crunchy, juicy or spicy.
items.explanation: A good short talk answers every part of the question and uses describing words so listeners can imagine the food.

items.prompt: Read this verse aloud. Use your voice to show how the kite moves.
items.readText:
Up, up it went above the town,
Above the roofs of red and brown.
It danced and dipped, it swooped and spun,
A small red bird against the sun.

criteria.label: I read at a good speed, not too fast
I used my voice to show the kite moving
I paused at the end of each line

hints: Read it quietly to yourself first.
Let your voice rise on up, up and dance on the action words.
items.explanation: Reading with expression means changing your voice to match the words, like going higher for up, up.

items.prompt: Explain how to do something you are good at, like tying your shoelaces. Use first, next, then and finally.

criteria.label: I explained the steps in the right order
I used order words like first, next and finally
I spoke clearly so a listener could follow

hints: Think through the steps before you start.
Say one step at a time.
items.explanation: Good spoken instructions give one step at a time, in order, with order words to help the listener.

items.prompt: Retell a story you know well in about one minute. Tell the beginning, the middle and the end.

criteria.label: I told the beginning, the middle and the end
I said who was in the story and what the problem was
I used my voice to make it interesting

hints: Choose a story you know really well.
Say who is in it, what goes wrong and how it ends.
items.explanation: A good retelling keeps the main events in order and leaves out small details.

items.prompt: Give a short talk about an animal you like. Share some facts about it, then say why you like it.

criteria.label: I gave some true facts about the animal
I said why I like it, with a reason
I spoke clearly and looked up from any notes

hints: Plan your facts first, such as where it lives and what it eats.
End with: I like this animal because...
items.explanation: A short talk is clear when it gives facts first and ends with your own opinion and a reason.

items.prompt: A new pupil is joining your class. Describe your school and explain how to get from the gate to the library.

criteria.label: I gave the directions in order
I used position words like next to, past and opposite

hints: Picture yourself walking in through the gate.
Use words like turn left, go past and next to.
items.explanation: Clear directions describe each part of the route in order, with position words that a new pupil can follow.
